findings.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection below target; cost-of-living distress and court enforcement delays threaten further deterioration
findings.detail: Council Tax achieved 27.50% collection against profiled target of 27.70% (0.20% shortfall); Business Rates achieved 26.53% against 26.43% target. Material underlying pressures: cost-of-living creating significant financial distress for residents and businesses, and HM Court unable to provide regular enforcement dates. These factors suggest collection challenges may persist or worsen.
findings.matters: Collection rates below target reduce available cash and may require bad debt provision increases. Court enforcement constraints coupled with cost-of-living pressures indicate collection challenges may be structural rather than temporary.
findings.figures: Council Tax: 27.50% vs 27.70% profiled target; Business Rates: 26.53% vs 26.43% target
findings.quote: Whilst the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) were rebased for 2026/27, the in-year collection remains challenging. The ongoing cost of living challenge is resulting in significant financial distress for large numbers of customers, making payment of increased Council tax demands problematic. HM Court service are also unable to provide regular court dates to support smooth enforcement.

findings.headline: HRA tenant rent arrears deteriorating: up to 1.49% of annual rental income from 1.15% year-on-year
findings.detail: Rent arrears increased by 0.34 percentage points. While the council incorporates bad debt provision and monitors arrears tightly, the upward trend reflects cost-of-living pressures on tenants. Continued deterioration could require higher bad debt provisions and further strain HRA finances.
findings.matters: Deteriorating rent collection indicates tenant financial stress and reduces reliable HRA income. This compounds existing deficits and could necessitate higher bad debt provisions, further pressuring service sustainability.
findings.figures: HRA rent arrears: 1.15% (prior year) → 1.49% (current), increase of 0.34 percentage points
findings.quote: Current tenant rent arrears rose from 1.15% to 1.49% of annual rental income over the past year.

findings.headline: HRA stock condition survey (91.5% complete) may identify additional capital investment requirements above budget
findings.detail: The housing stock condition survey remains 91.5% incomplete. The council acknowledges completion may result in additional capital spend beyond current budget. Given the HRA is already running a £456k deficit, any material findings would create further pressure on constrained finances.
findings.matters: Unquantified cost pressures emerging on a service already running deficits represents material financial uncertainty. Completion of this survey could reveal substantial additional needs, further straining finances.
findings.figures: Survey 91.5% complete; no estimate provided for potential additional spend
findings.quote: The stock condition survey is 91.5% complete which may result in additional spend being required above the current level of investment included in the budget.

findings.headline: Supported housing cost gap creating increasing pressures on General Fund with no quantified solution identified
findings.detail: The council identifies a structural cost gap: the difference between actual cost to provide supported housing (via charities and private sector) and recoverable housing benefit creates increasing General Fund pressure. The scale of this gap is unquantified and no mitigation strategy is articulated beyond acknowledging the pressure.
findings.matters: This is a non-discretionary service cost for a rising demand (homelessness). The unquantified financial gap with no identified solution represents open-ended exposure that could grow and impact General Fund sustainability.
findings.figures: No figures provided for scale of gap or solution
findings.quote: the gap between the cost to the Council of the supported housing premium (when the housing is provided by charities and the private sector) and the lower level of housing benefit that can be reclaimed is creating increasing pressures on the GF.

findings.headline: Capital resources are depleted and cannot be easily replaced from revenue or future capital receipts
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that capital resources (excluding borrowing) are now depleted and cannot be easily replaced. This constraint is particularly acute given the concurrent £500k reduction in Right-to-Buy receipts. All future capital investment is now constrained to available borrowing or new revenue-generated funding.
findings.matters: Depleted capital resources constrain the council's ability to maintain assets, fund regeneration, or respond to infrastructure needs without increased borrowing. This is a material strategic constraint on the council's investment flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital receipts reduced by £500k (from £2.2m to £1.7m); capital resources identified as depleted
findings.quote: Capital resources (other than borrowing) are depleted and will not be easily replaced from revenue contributions or capital receipts.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account deficit worsened by £173k in Q1 to £456k, requiring £455k drawdown from reserves
findings.detail: The HRA deficit deteriorated from the budgeted £283k to a £456k projected outturn. The primary driver is the £265k interest cost on Right-to-Buy receipt repayments—a governance failure rather than market condition. This requires a £455k contribution from the Housing Initiatives Reserve to cover the operational deficit.
findings.matters: A worsening deficit driven by delivery failure rather than external factors, in Q1 of the year, raises sustainability concerns. Reliance on reserve drawdowns to fund operational deficits reduces financial flexibility and may signal the HRA cannot achieve balance without further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: HRA deficit: £283k (budget) → £456k (Q1 forecast), adverse variance of £173k; reserve contribution £455k
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account – £173k net adverse variances identified, leading to an increased deficit of £456k forecast for 2026/27.

findings.headline: £505k of historic Right-to-Buy receipts must be repaid to MHCLG due to failure to spend within statutory deadlines; interest charge of £265k
findings.detail: Following audit, the council identified £505k of retained Right-to-Buy receipts allocated to projects from 2021/22 onwards that were not spent within prescribed timescales and must be repaid to MHCLG. Interest at base rate plus 8% (totalling £265k) will be charged and funded from the Housing Initiatives Reserve. This reduces available capital receipts balance from £2.2m to £1.7m, directly reducing capital funding capacity.
findings.matters: This represents both loss of capital resources and a governance failure in project delivery. Failure to deploy capital resources on time indicates weak project management or delivery, a material concern for lenders assessing financial control.
findings.figures: £505k repayment required, £265k interest charge (base rate plus 8%), capital receipts balance reduced from £2.2m to £1.7m
findings.quote: Following a recent review and audit of the receipts allocated to projects dating back to 2021/22 it has been identified that £505k of historic receipts were not spent in the allotted time and will need to be repaid to MHCLG.

findings.headline: Dover has £91 million in short-term cash flow borrowing from 22 different public sector lenders
findings.detail: The council lists extensive short-term loans from Greater Manchester Combined Authority, West Midlands Combined Authority, London boroughs, individual councils, and other authorities including Humberside Fire Authority, London Treasury Liquidity Fund LP, and Castlepoint BC. Every short-term loan is designated as being for 'Strategic cash flow purposes', indicating the borrowing finances working capital and liquidity management.
findings.matters: This scale and diversity of short-term borrowing exposes the council to refinancing risk if lender appetite changes or if access to these unsecured loans tightens, and indicates the council is dependent on rolling over debt across multiple counterparties.
findings.figures: £91,000,000 short-term principal outstanding at 1 April 2025; £55,500,000 repaid during 2025/26; 22 separate loans with interest rates 4.15% to 5.80%

findings.matters: A sharp unexplained reduction in working capital reserves within a month signals either capital deployment, refinancing activity, or a council outflow that requires context. A lender needs to understand what drove this drawdown.

findings.detail: The report identifies that as Universal Credit rolls out, Dover will lose its primary recovery mechanism (deductions from ongoing Housing Benefit). Recovery from Universal Credit will be 'at a significantly reduced rate' and the report explicitly flags this as 'a future challenge'. No mitigation strategy is detailed. Current outstanding HB overpayments stand at £1.354m.
findings.matters: Housing Benefit overpayment recovery is a material income stream; if the collection mechanism deteriorates substantially during UC transition, this represents a future income loss and operational risk.

The Section 151 Officer is aware and bad debt provisions have been applied, but 'this will likely result in an increased level of write offs in this area in 2026/2027'. The magnitude of affected cases is not disclosed.
findings.matters: A material system defect preventing proper debt finalisation indicates control weaknesses in accounts closure, and creates unquantified future liability from unprocessed write-offs.
findings.figures: Affected case numbers not disclosed; impact deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: There are debts that are due to be written off but due to a current system limitation within the current financial system, no transactional action can be taken to finalise these cases... This will likely result in an increased level of write offs in this area in 2026/2027

findings.paper_title: Annual Write Off Report for PartnershipOne 2025-26
findings.headline: Business Rates write-offs more than doubled to £828k, collection rate fell to 96.36%, and outstanding debt nearly tripled to £2.54m
findings.detail: Business Rates write-offs jumped from £400k in 2024/25 to £828k in 2025/26. Collection rate fell from 97.77% to 96.36%, and outstanding debt spiked from £933k to £2.54m. The spike reflects a council project identifying historic unpaid rates as irrecoverable, including 19 write-offs above £10k featuring multiple business liquidations (Poundland £116k, Cow and Bird £79k) and dissolutions.
findings.matters: Large write-offs coupled with deteriorating collection rates and accumulated outstanding debt suggest either underlying economic distress in the local business community or prior collection process weaknesses now being addressed.
findings.quote: Write offs in 2025/26 totalled £827,949.93. In comparison, the figure for 2024/2025 was £400,373.02.

findings.paper_title: Annual Write Off Report for PartnershipOne 2025-26
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate declined 0.87% while the council increased charges by 7.72%, pushing outstanding debt up 23% to £4.07m
findings.detail: Despite raising Council Tax charges by 7.72%, collection rates fell from 96.46% in-year to 95.97% in 2025/26. Outstanding debt rose materially from £3.31m in 2024/25 to £4.07m in 2025/26 — a £760k increase. This signals residents are struggling to pay at higher charge levels, reducing the reliability of the council's primary revenue source.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the council's most predictable funding stream; declining collections while charges rise indicates resident difficulty paying and suggests future revenue headwinds.
findings.figures: Collection decrease 0.87%, charge increase 7.72%, outstanding debt £4.07m (2024/25: £3.31m)
findings.quote: There has been a decrease in Council Tax collection of 0.87%, leading to an overall increase for in year, year end balances owed when compared with 2025/26 of £4.07m from £3.31m in 2024/25.

findings.detail: The council's original budget for temporary borrowing interest was £3.4m, but the report flags that actual costs "may slightly increase" due to capital projects including Deal Leisure Centre and ongoing housing developments. The council says it will monitor and report further if adjustment is needed.
findings.matters: A budget caveat in July indicates the MTFP may not have accurately forecasted borrowing costs for the year, which could require reserve drawdown or other budget action if not resolved.
findings.figures: £3.4m budget; cost may increase
findings.quote: The original budget for 2026/27 for temporary borrowing interest was £3.4m. The cost for the year may slightly increase due capital projects (Deal Leisure Centre) and housing developments and purchases. The position will continue to be monitored and will be included in future reports if needed.

findings.paper_title: TM Q1 2026-27 Cabinet Report for Governance
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing increased by £8 million in the first quarter to fund housing and capital projects
findings.detail: Short-term cashflow borrowing rose from £55.5m to £63.5m between April and June 2026, representing a 14% quarterly increase. This was driven by housing development projects being funded through borrowing rather than from reserves or capital grants. Cashflow volatility also contributed to the higher borrowing need.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing is interest-rate sensitive and volatile; a sharp increase in capital funding through this route signals dependency on money markets and exposure to rate movements, which a lender would want to understand the duration and sustainability of.
findings.figures: £55.5m to £63.5m, £8m increase
findings.quote: Short term cashflow borrowing increased from £55.5m to £63.5m due to housing development projects being funded through borrowing and fluctuations in the cash flow requirements.

findings.headline: Council holds £55m in short-term loans from other local authorities
findings.detail: At year-end March 2026, Dover held £55 million in short-term loans from other local authorities as part of its cash management strategy, representing material short-term financing exposure.
findings.matters: Large short-term debt portfolio carries refinancing risk and indicates dependence on inter-authority lending for cash flow management
findings.figures: £55 million in short-term loans at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026, the Council had £55 million in short term loans with other Local Authorities as part of the Council's strategic cash management objectives.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs exceeded budget by £894k due to housing development investment
findings.detail: The council incurred additional short-term borrowing costs of £894k above the budget estimate of £1,091k, an 82% overspend. The increase was driven by reduced available funds for inter-authority lending and further investment in housing property development.
findings.matters: Significant unbudgeted increase in debt servicing costs indicates either unexpected cash flow pressures or capital commitments consuming more resources than anticipated
findings.figures: £894k increase over budget estimate of £1,091k
findings.quote: A reduction in available funds for inter-authority lending and further investment in the development of housing properties has caused a £894k increase in the cost of borrowing in 2025/26 from the original budget estimate of £1,091k.

findings.headline: Council exceeded prudential indicator limit for interest rate risk in 2025-26
findings.detail: Dover did not comply with prudential indicator 9.6 regarding exposure to interest rate risk. The actual exposure was £693k when the council's target for 2025-26 was £500k. The council has amended the limit to £750k for 2026-27.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with prudential indicators represents a failure of key financial controls and raises questions about treasury management oversight
findings.figures: £693k actual exposure vs £500k target for 2025-26
findings.quote: The Council has operated within the Prudential Indicators in compliance with the Council's Treasury Management Practices on all areas except for the indicator for the Council's exposure to interest rate risk (Appendix 1 paragraph 9.6.1). This shows that were the interest rates increase or decrease by 1% the difference between the interest receivable and payable would be £693k whereas the target for 2025/26 is £500k.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream have improved from 15.8% to 10.9%, but are budgeted to rise to 13.5% as HRA borrowing impacts future years
findings.detail: The actual financing cost burden improved significantly from £3.1m (2024/25) to £2.4m (2025/26), despite increased capital expenditure. However, the budget projects financing costs will increase to £2.8m (13.5% of revenue stream) in 2026/27, reflecting the impact of new HRA borrowing beginning to service.
findings.matters: Financing costs as a percentage of revenue stream is a key indicator of financial sustainability for lenders. While currently improving, the trajectory is expected to reverse as new debt servicing costs impact the revenue budget
findings.figures: Financing costs: £3.1m (2024/25), £2.4m (2025/26), £2.8m (2026/27); As proportion of net revenue stream: 15.8%, 10.9%, 13.5% respectively
findings.quote: The net annual charge is known as financing costs; this is compared to the net revenue stream i.e. the amount funded from Council Tax, business rates and general government grants.

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure is planned to fall to zero in 2027/28, having been £9.8m in 2026/27 and £18.5m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme is projected to end entirely by 2027/28. The council's capital strategy is increasingly focused on HRA housing investment. Current General Fund projects include Dover Beacon (£12.6m) and the Tides Leisure Centre replacement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether zero General Fund capital spending is planned completion of the current programme or reflects inability to fund ongoing capital renewal needs in services
findings.quote: The main General Fund capital projects to date have included Dover Beacon Project, and major restoration works on Maison Dieu (Dover Town Hall), Tides Leisure Centre replacement, and Deal Pier structural repairs.

findings.headline: Debt is projected to increase from £10.9m to £82.4m between March 2026 and March 2027, driven by capital expenditure financing
findings.detail: The significant increase in debt reflects the HRA capital programme financing strategy. The debt spike is consistent with the Capital Financing Requirement growing from £160.7m to £182.6m over the same period. Current borrowing stands at £118.1m against an Authorised Limit of £338.5m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and its position relative to legal borrowing limits. The 655% projected increase in debt in a single year represents a major financial commitment that must be serviceable from the council's revenue stream
findings.figures: Debt: £10.9m (31.3.2026), £82.4m (31.3.2027), £40.9m (31.3.2028); Capital Financing Requirement: £160.7m to £182.6m; Current borrowing £118.1m against Authorised Limit £338.5m
findings.quote: Statutory guidance is that debt should remain below the capital financing requirement, except in the short term. The Council has complied and expects to continue to comply with this requirement in the medium term as is shown below.

findings.headline: HRA capital expenditure is planned to increase dramatically to £83.3m in 2026/27, up from £23.9m actual in 2025/26 - a 248% increase
findings.detail: The council is pursuing an ambitious housing development programme. In 2025/26, it delivered 63 additional homes. The HRA Affordable Housing Development Project is budgeted at £21.1m. This represents a major strategic shift in capital allocation toward council housing provision.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council's capital commitments and debt trajectory. A near-tripling of HRA capital spending signals major new borrowing requirements and future repayment obligations that will impact the council's revenue budget
findings.figures: HRA capital expenditure: £23.9m (2025/26 actual) to £83.3m (2026/27 budget); HRA Affordable Housing Development Project £21.1m; 63 homes delivered in 2025/26
findings.quote: HRA capital expenditure is recorded separately. The Council delivered 63 additional homes to our housing stock, including temporary and general needs accommodation. Additional homes are in the pipeline, as part of our ambitious multi-million-pound programme to provide much-needed homes for local people.

findings.headline: Borrowing maturity concentrated in short-term – half of debt due within 12 months
findings.detail: The council holds £59.4m (50.3%) of its £118.1m total borrowing maturing within 12 months, creating material refinancing exposure. Short-term borrowing increased from £37m to £55.5m in the year. Late-year short-term borrowing costs surged to 5-7% from earlier 4-4.5% levels, and this concentration means the council must refinance roughly half its debt in coming months at prevailing market rates.
findings.matters: High concentration of near-term debt maturity creates refinancing risk – if rates remain elevated or market conditions tighten, the council faces forced reissuance of half its debt book at potentially significantly higher cost than its longer-term fixed portfolio
findings.figures: £59.4m of £118.1m total borrowing due within 12 months (50.3%); formal short-term borrowing £55.5m, up £18.5m year-on-year; late-year rates reached 5-7%
findings.quote: At 31st March 2026 the Council held £55.5m of short-term loans, an increase of £18.5m to 31 st March 2025, as part of its strategy for funding previous years' capital programmes.

findings.headline: Forecast borrowing requirement to rise 58% from £74m to £116.9m by 2028
findings.detail: The liability benchmark, which estimates the minimum borrowing the council must hold to fund its capital and revenue plans, is forecast to escalate rapidly. Actual borrowing need at 31 March 2026 was £74.0m; this is forecast to reach £104.9m by 2027 and £116.9m by 2028. This 58% two-year growth trajectory indicates material expansion of capital commitments or emerging revenue pressures ahead.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising forecast borrowing needs suggest the council's spending plans are outpacing revenue generation, raising questions about sustainability and future refinancing capacity – core assessment points for lenders
findings.figures: Liability benchmark forecast: £74.0m actual (31/3/26), £104.9m forecast (31/3/27), £116.9m forecast (31/3/28)

findings.headline: Current tenant arrears as a percentage of rental income rose from 1.15% to 1.49%, with staffing recruitment difficulties preventing mitigation
findings.detail: Current tenant arrears increased from £293,858 to £398,751. The council identifies two drivers: the cost of living crisis reducing tenants' ability to pay rent, and challenges recruiting specialist benefits advisors who help tenants maximize income to support rent payments.
findings.matters: Rising collection failure indicates weakening HRA financial resilience and tenant vulnerability, with staffing constraints preventing the council from mitigating cost-of-living impacts.

findings.matters: Prudential indicators exist to ensure councils manage debt within intended risk tolerances; exceeding the interest rate risk metric signals the debt/investment mix is exposed to more interest rate volatility than the council intended, which affects financial resilience and lender confidence.
